faq: Do you store passwords or secrets?
Keys and secrets are stored hashed or in your environment settings, never in the code. We do not ask for your passwords. You create access for us inside your own hosting account.
Can you add authentication to an API that is already live?
Yes. We plan a safe switch so existing users keep working, for example a grace period with warnings. We confirm the rollout plan with you before changing anything.
What is the difference between API keys and OAuth?
Keys suit simple server-to-server use. OAuth lets your customers allow another app to act for them without sharing a password. We recommend one after hearing how your API is used.
Is this a full security audit?
No. This service covers sign-in and permissions on the API. A wider review of how accounts are stored and protected is a separate service in our user accounts group.
desc:
API authentication with keys, tokens and scopes decides who can reach your data and what they can do once inside. Ecom Swift LLC adds sign-in to your API, from simple API keys to token sign-in and OAuth, and tests the failure cases as well.

## What is API authentication?

API authentication is the check an API makes to learn who is calling before it answers. The caller shows a credential, such as a key or a token, and the API either accepts it or refuses the request. Authorization is the next step: it decides which actions that caller may perform.

Without both steps, an API answers anyone who finds its address. Customer records, orders and internal tools become reachable by scrapers, competitors and curious strangers.

## Why an open API becomes a problem quickly

An unprotected endpoint rarely stays unnoticed. Automated scanners look for open routes all the time, and a single leaked address can expose every record behind it. Even when nobody attacks you, a partner can break something by accident, and without a credential you cannot tell which partner it was.

Good sign-in also gives you control. You can give each partner their own key, see which key made a call, and switch one key off without disturbing anyone else. That is what lets you share an API with outside developers without worrying about every one of them.

## How good authentication helps your business

Sign-in does not make an API faster, but it makes it safe to open up, and that is where the value comes from. Partners and customers will only build on an API they can trust with their own data. Clear error messages for bad keys also cut support questions, because developers can see at once whether the problem is a typo, an expired token or a missing permission.

Scopes protect you from your own mistakes. A key that can only read orders cannot delete them, so a bug in a partner's code stays small. Easy key revocation turns a leaked credential from an emergency into a small chore.

## What a well-built API sign-in includes

- An API key or token check on every route, with no forgotten endpoints.
- Keys stored as hashes, so a database leak does not reveal usable keys.
- Token sign-in with a short expiry and a refresh step for your own app.
- Permission scopes that limit each key or token to specific actions.
- OAuth 2.0 for third-party apps that act on behalf of your users.
- A simple way to create, list and revoke keys without touching the database.
- Clear, consistent error responses for missing, wrong, expired and under-privileged credentials.
- Automated tests for requests that must be blocked, not only those that must pass.
- Short security notes that explain how it works for the next developer.

## How we add sign-in to your API

We start by reading your routes and deciding which approach fits who calls them. Partners with server code usually do well with API keys. Your own web or mobile app usually needs token sign-in. Outside apps that act for your users call for OAuth.

Then we add the checks to every route, set up safe key storage and write the create and revoke tools. We define the scopes with you, apply them per route and test what happens when a request is wrong. The Basic, Standard and Premium packages differ in how far this goes: from keys on every route, to tokens with scopes, to OAuth and a page where customers manage their own keys.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Give every partner or app its own key so you can trace and revoke it alone.
- Grant the smallest set of scopes that a caller needs.
- Set expiry on tokens and plan for key rotation.
- Return the same style of error for every failure.
- Test blocked requests as carefully as allowed ones.

**Avoid:**
- Sharing one key between several customers.
- Putting keys in front-end code, URLs or public repositories.
- Storing keys or secrets in plain text.
- Returning detailed error text that helps an attacker guess what failed.
- Treating sign-in as a full security audit, because it covers access, not every other weakness.

## Who this service is for

A software company opening its API to partners for the first time needs keys and scopes before the first partner connects. A small team with a live API that has no sign-in at all needs protection added without breaking existing callers. A product that wants third-party apps to connect to its users' accounts needs OAuth and a place for customers to manage access.

## What we need from you

Send us a description of who will call the API, the list of routes or the OpenAPI file, and the repository or hosting details. We work in your own account as a developer or collaborator user, so you keep full control. We never need your passwords, and we never ask you to share secrets in a message. If a secret is needed for testing, we agree a safe way to handle a test value together.
